title: Sending and taking
hookLine: second point: tonglen, riding the breath

lines: POINT TWO TURNS IT UPSIDE DOWN.
TAKE IN THE HEAVY, SEND OUT THE LIGHT.
cards: Breathe in the good stuff, breathe out the bad. Calm in, stress out.
It's the instruction at the end of a yoga class, in a relaxation app, from a kind nurse before a shot, and it makes sense: keep what helps, let go of what hurts.

Point two of the seven points of mind training turns it upside down. Breathe in what is heavy, someone's pain, someone's fear. Breathe out whatever is light and good, your ease, your warmth, and send it to them.
It sounds backward. It's meant to.

teach.b: You first met tonglen on day three hundred ten; here it sits inside its point. First, the name. Tonglen: tong, sending or giving, and len, taking.
It belongs to point two, the main practice, training the awakened heart, the wish to wake up for the sake of others. Second, the instruction.

teach.h: TAKE IN ON THE BREATH, SEND OUT ON IT.
teach.b: One slogan says, in effect, practice sending and taking alternately, and let the two ride the breath. On the in-breath, the student takes in another's suffering, which some teachers suggest picturing as dark, heavy smoke.
On the out-breath, the student sends out happiness, health, whatever good they have, often pictured as cool, bright light. The breath carries it like a horse carries a rider.
Third, where to start. Another slogan says to begin the taking with oneself.
Teachers suggest starting with your own pain, or the pain of someone you love, before widening to a stranger, and only later to someone difficult.
Nobody walks into a gym on the first day and loads the heaviest weight on the rack. Fourth, what it's working on. The habit underneath ordinary life is grab the good, push away the bad.
Tonglen trains the opposite reflex, and teachers say what it wears down is self-cherishing, that quiet voice saying me first.
It isn't a substitute for actually helping. Practitioners describe it as training the heart, so that when the moment comes to help, the heart is already pointed the right way.

how: Tibetan Buddhist practitioners practice tonglen by imagining taking in others' suffering on the in-breath and sending out happiness on the out-breath, usually beginning with themselves or someone close and widening from there.

o: giving away your things and taking only what you need
breathing in others' pain and breathing out ease to them
breathing in calm and breathing out your own stress

games.q: sending and taking: tap the pairs.

s: tonglen breathes in calm and breathes out stress
it's the reverse: take in what's heavy, send out what's light and good.
a slogan says sending and taking should ride the breath
the two are practiced alternately, carried by the breath like a rider on a horse.
teachers suggest starting with the most difficult person you know
a slogan says to begin the taking with oneself, then widen.

games.q: you sit down to try tonglen for the first time. whose suffering does the slogan say to take in first?
games.why: a slogan says to begin the taking with oneself. teachers then widen it to loved ones, strangers, and only later difficult people.

practice: Bring to mind something heavy in you right now, a worry, an ache; breathe it in, and on the out-breath send yourself some ease, for a few rounds.
Then think of someone you love who's struggling, breathe in their trouble, and breathe out whatever warmth you have toward them.
Teachers often give this longer; if it gets too much, come back to just the breath, since nothing is required.

wordCard.voice: Sending and taking. Tonglen: taking in others' suffering on the in-breath, sending out happiness on the out-breath. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: riding the breath. In with the heavy, out with the light. Breathe easy.
